arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: General Sauer argued for the government and asked the Court to reverse the lower decision. The government's core claim was that the Citizenship Clause does not grant birthright citizenship to children of temporary visitors or undocumented immigrants. The approved record does not state the other side's requested result or detailed contentions.

The justices tested assumptions on both history and practicality. Chief Justice Roberts asked about birth tourism and about extrapolating narrow exceptions to exclude a large class. Justice Barrett probed how a domicile rule works for foundlings and unknown parental intent. Justice Jackson asked why the amendment's text would omit parents if parental status controls.
The case was submitted after argument, meaning the justices will decide it later.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The case, Trump v. Barbara, asks who counts as a citizen from birth under the Fourteenth Amendment. The government argues the Citizenship Clause does not grant birthright citizenship to children of temporary visitors or undocumented immigrants. The other side says the Constitution grants citizenship to nearly everyone born here.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: The justices tested several assumptions. Chief Justice Roberts asked how common birth tourism is and whether narrow exceptions can justify excluding a large class. Justice Barrett pressed how a domicile rule would work, including for foundlings and parents whose plans to stay are unknown.

Several justices focused on Wong Kim Ark, an old case about citizenship. Justice Alito pressed why domicile appears in that case's stated question and holding. Chief Justice Roberts questioned dismissing the repeated mention of domicile there. Justice Barrett also tested how a domicile rule would handle a U. S. citizen giving birth here while living abroad.
